To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) The growing modes problem in the case of a background geometry that decomposes into two maximally symmetric spaces can be solved by means of an appropriate generalization of the standard technique based on the separation of variables in the Fourier modes; 2) The scalar and tensor inomogeneities in this kind of backgrounds are described by gauge-invariant variables that can be written in terms of two scalar fields and one vector field, respectively; 3) The growing mode problem can be solved in

in the context of the dimensional decoupling scenario the scalar and tensor fluctuations are not independent of each other, that in the contracting phase the scalar modes grow more than the gravity waves and that the amplitude of the gravity waves background is sensitive to the internal geometry and dynamics of the compactified dimensions.

the growing mode problem in a background geometry that naturally decomposes into a direct product of two Eucledian spaces can be solved by a suitable gauge invariant treatment and that, in the presence of inhomogeneities that depend on the internal spatial dimensions, the spectral amplitude of gravity waves produced during the evolution of the Universe depends on the typical frequency scale of the internal excitatons.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the study of scalar and tensor perturbations of a cosmological model in which the spatial sections of the background geometry naturally decompose into the direct product $\mathbb{R}^{3}\times\mathbb{S}^{n}$, where $n>1$.

the possibility that the scalar and tensor perturbations of a background geometry whose spatial part decomposes into a direct product of two spaces of different dimensionality, can be described by means of a suitable decomposition of the metric perturbations in the internal and external directions.
the study of the scalar and gravitational waves produced in the context of dimensional decoupled models of the very early universe.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the amplitude of the gravity wave fluctuations depends on both the internal and external geometry of the compactified manifold, a result that is expected to hold also for more general situations.
the internal geometry is not only a source of the inhomogeneities in the external geometry but it also affects their dynamics and their amplitude.
the scalar and tensor perturbations are not completely decoupled and, in general, they can be affected by the internal degrees of freedom of the compactified space-time.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the internal geometry is not only a source of scalar inhomogeneities but also a source of gravity waves.

the amplitude of the stochastic background of gravity waves is enhanced if the compactification scale is of the order of the Hubble scale and the internal frequency is of the order $H$, where $H$ is the Hubble constant.

we are able to compute the scalar and tensor perturbations in a general situation in which the spatial section is a direct product of a $d$ dimensional space-time with scale factor $ a(\ensuremath{\tau})$ and a $n$ dimensional maximally symmetric Eucleadian manifold with scale factor $ b(\ensuremath{\nu})$ and we are able to find a gauge-invariant formulation for these perturbations.
The main takeaway from our work is that

in the presence of internal dimensions, the gravity waves spectrum can be significantly modified by the internal dynamics, even in the limit where the internal dimensions are small compared to the typical wavelength of the external geometry.
the amplitude of the tensor modes can be significantly enhanced by the internal degrees of freedom.
the dimensional decoupling can be used in order to produce anisotropic backgrounds which can be employed as toy models for the study of the scalar and the tensor inhomogeneites of the early Universe.
